paragraphs.source_en: Kangetsu said, “It was already nine o’clock. Now, through the long autumn night, I was to climb those eight hundred meters of mountain path all alone, to a place called Odaira. I am naturally very timid, and ordinarily I would have been beside myself with fear; but once one fixes one’s whole mind on a single thing, wonders occur, and no fear whatsoever arises, not even as a thought. My mind held only one idea: I wanted to play the violin. Strange, isn’t it? This place called Odaira lies on the south side of Koshin Mountain; on a clear day, when one climbs up there, the town can be taken in at a glance through the red pines. It is a flat stretch with a superb view. Yes, it is a good hundred tsubo in area, and in the middle stands a great rock about the size of eight tatami mats; to the north it adjoins Unonuma Pond, and around the pond grow camphor trees so large it would take three men to embrace them. Since it is deep in the mountains, there is only one hut for collecting camphor, and the area around the pond is uncanny even in broad daylight. Fortunately, the engineers had cut a path there for their maneuvers, so the climb was not too hard. At last I reached the top of the great rock, spread out my blanket, and somehow managed to sit down at its edge. It was the first time I had climbed there on such a cold night, and after I sat on the rock and calmed down a little, the desolation all around slowly seeped through my whole body and mind. In such circumstances, the only thing that unsettles a man is the feeling of fear; so if that feeling is removed, what remains is only a bright, keen, ethereal air. I sat there in a daze for about twenty minutes, and for some reason I began to feel as though I alone were living in a palace of crystal. And I, living alone in that crystal palace, my body—no, not only my body, but my mind and my soul as well—seemed to be made entirely of agar, becoming perfectly clear and transparent. Whether I myself lived inside the crystal palace, or the crystal palace lay within me, I could no longer tell.”

paragraphs.source_en: Kangetsu said, “After that, having come back to my senses, I looked all around, and the whole of Koshin Mountain was utterly still, without even a sound the size of a raindrop. I thought, ‘How strange. What was that sound just now? If it was a human voice, it was much too shrill; if it was a bird’s cry, it was much too loud; could it have been a monkey? But there should be no monkeys in this neighborhood. What was it? What was it?’ No sooner had this question arisen in my mind than I wanted to explain it, and then all the things that had just been so silent suddenly whirled about in my head, confused and clamorous, like the people of the capital thrown into frenzy on the occasion of welcoming His Highness the Duke of Connaught. Before long, every pore in my body suddenly opened, and like hairy shins sprayed with shochu, all those guests known as courage, nerve, reason, and composure went hissing off into thin air. My heart began dancing the suteteko beneath my ribs, and both my legs started trembling with a sound like the hum of a kite. This was unbearable. I instantly pulled the blanket over my head, tucked the violin under my arm, leapt unsteadily down from the great rock, ran straight down the eight hundred meters of mountain path to the foot of the hill, went home, crawled into my bedding, and lay down. Even now, thinking back on it, I have never had such a hair-raising experience, I tell you, Tofu!”
